Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve this as an ordinary local field update rather than a dramatic story, and keep the episode self-contained so a reader can understand what sign was involved, where it stood, and why the replacement was being considered without needing other reports. The sign is on the North Fork Trail near the split for Alder Spur and the Creek Overlook. The trail junction is about two miles from the west gate, and the replacement work takes place on a Thursday in late May. Use those details as the setting, and do not turn the update into a general guide to trail maintenance.

Explain that the old Cedar Notch sign had faded lettering and a lower corner that had split around one of its mounting holes after several wet seasons. The trail crew had noticed the damage on two separate inspections, but the sign was still standing and could still be read at close range. Describe why the crew scheduled a replacement before the summer visitor period without suggesting that the trail had been closed or that anyone had been hurt. The crew brought a new cedar board with dark green lettering and kept the arrow layout and wording consistent with the trail map. The update should distinguish the visible damage from the crew's reason for acting and not imply that the old sign was an immediate danger.

Include concrete details about the morning work, but keep the account modest. The crew reached the junction at 8:20 and carried the board and hand tools from the west gate rather than bringing a vehicle onto the trail. The ground was damp from overnight rain, and the creek was running higher than it had during the earlier inspection. Two crew members worked at the post while a third stayed near the junction to answer hikers and keep the path clear. Mention that no powered equipment was used and that the old board was lowered by hand. Do not add an exact work duration because none was recorded.

Show what was checked before the new board went up. The crew compared its arrows with the current map and confirmed that Alder Spur continued east while Creek Overlook remained to the south. Describe the post as leaning slightly toward the trail but firm when tested by hand. One mounting bolt had rust on its exposed end, and the other hardware was usable. State that the crew replaced the damaged board and the rusty bolt while leaving the post in place and reusing the sound hardware. Do not suggest that they rebuilt the junction or changed either route.

Include a short numbered section in the update with these three checks in this order, and keep each one tied to what the crew actually observed:
1. Confirm the two route arrows against the current map.
2. Check the post by hand before attaching the board.
3. Look over the finished sign from the trail approach.
Use those checks to make the field account easy to follow rather than presenting them as a general safety rule. The last check should say that both route names could be read from the approach and that the board sat level when the crew stepped back. Do not claim that the sign was tested in poor light or from every direction.

Include one ordinary reported quote from Mara Ellis, the crew lead, who said, “The old post is still solid, so we can keep the work to the sign and its hardware.” Place the quote after the account of the post inspection, and make clear that it is her observation at the junction rather than a policy statement. Do not add another speaker or turn the quote into a claim about future maintenance. Mara also noted that the route map had not changed and that the crew had brought the wording from the current map for the new board. Keep that detail separate from the quote, and do not invent a map revision date.

Cover the limits of the work as well as what was completed. The crew did not move the post, cut vegetation, alter the trail surface, or change the route markers farther along either branch. No additional damage was found on the nearby markers during the brief look from the junction, but do not describe that as a full survey. The crew carried the removed board and the rusty bolt back to the west gate for disposal and left no tools or materials at the site. Say that the update concerns only the Cedar Notch junction and the replacement completed there.

Make the account chronological from the arrival through the inspection, attachment of the board, and walk back to the gate. The crew paused while two hikers passed through the junction and answered a question about which branch reached Creek Overlook. Do not give the hikers names or invent their reaction. Keep the weather detail limited to overnight rain and damp ground, and do not add a forecast or a claim about how long the sign will last. The new lettering should be described as dark green and legible at the junction, but do not promise that it can be seen under every condition.

End with the crew's assessment of the finished work and retain its conditions and scope. The crew considered the replacement complete because the new board was level, its wording and arrows matched the current map, and the post remained firm during the hand check. Their assessment applies to the sign at the North Fork junction on that visit only. Mention that a later inspection would still be needed as part of the usual seasonal checks without setting a date or suggesting that a defect remained. The crew did not assess the condition of the full North Fork Trail or make a broader statement about signs elsewhere.

In the final paragraph, include distinct information about what happened after the check. The crew packed the hand tools, carried the removed board back to the west gate, and left the junction open for hikers. The update should finish with that account rather than repeat the assessment or add a recommendation, approval, or general summary. Keep the tone factual and local, and use connected paragraphs with the three requested checks as the only numbered section."}]
